segments.description: Introducing Peter Karunas, a performance strategist with over 30 years of experience, is the creator of My Success Map, a framework for achieving personal and professional goals. Combining success psychology with leadership principles, Peter empowers individuals and teams. In his session Mapping Success, Strategies for Performance and Leadership, he'll share tools to navigate challenges and drive success. Welcome Peter. Hi, I'm Peter Karunas and welcome to this video on My Success Map. In the next 15 minutes, I am excited to share with you a map to help you, your players and your team achieve success on and off court. And it's something that I've designed over the last 30 years and I'm really excited to be sharing it with you. We'll get into that shortly, but just thought I'd set the scene a little bit. I'm a strategist, coach, leader and motivator and for the last 13 years, 30 years, I've been working with people, teams and organizations internationally and nationally. I've had the opportunity to work with boards and CEOs all the way through to the front line in high performance and high risk environments. And my background is in psychology, organizational psychology and human factors. I completed my masters in that. And yeah, I'm really excited to share with you my success map, which I've used with people, teams and organizations to help me achieve success. Outside of my business experience, I'm a father and also a black belt in Brazilian jiu-jitsu. I have my club here in Adelaide, South Australia, about 15 to 20 students.

And yeah, I'll tell you a little bit about my background. I've also played sport at a high level previous to do in jiu-jitsu. I played Australian rules football at a reasonably high level. Legend has it that I was being scouted by the Bears Brisbane Lions, but yeah, that's a little bit about my background. I managed to captain the Glen Elk under 19s here in South Australia and went on to play division one in amateur league football. And yeah, just a little bit about my background and enjoy some success in football. So high performance in sport and business has been a part of my life and it's still part of my life. And that's a little bit about me. The context for today and I guess this session is I really am excited to share with you a map that I've designed with the help of my mentor over the over the years to help organizations, people and teams have a blueprint, a formula for how to achieve success. It's something that I believe know that you will use with your team, with your players, as I said, on court, off court to help you to achieve success. And whether that's about growing your business or retaining your team or setting a vision for success, whatever it is, this is really a map that helps put all those little parts together and help you to think about the things that you need to do to achieve success. And so what I'd like to do in the next 15 minutes, as I said, is to take you through it, talk to you a little bit about how I facilitate it as well.

And at the end of this, if you've got any questions, feel free to reach out to me. I trust that my details will be made available through this as well. I'm really excited to talk to you a little bit more about that if you've got any questions on it. Now, there is an attachment, which is my success map to this video. I was trying to work out how to actually show on teams, but I'm not that high performance in other areas, but not with video and an AV. So even though my brother's in that space, so go figure. But yes, there is an attachment that comes with this and it's my it is my success map. And yeah, welcome you to have a look at that. And you'll forgive me as I look at my agenda as we're working through. So before we get into my success map, what I'd like to just sort of set the scene on it. And when I am working with people, teams and organizations, the very first conversation that I have with them is to define success. Before we get into the actual map and how it works and how to build it, a conversation around how do we define success? I've got a definition of that for myself, but I think that's a really critical starting point. There's an author that as you're watching this, you may very well know, Stephen Covey, seven habits of highly effective people. And one of those habits he talks about is starting with the end in mind. And that really is a starting point for for myself for the work that I do with with clients and for them is to define very, very clearly.

What is success look like? What does it sound like? What does it feel like? And I think that's critical because the definition of that helps set up everything else that that then follows. And for me, my definition of success is it's not success in just one area. It's balance success across a range of areas that are important contextually. So at a life level, if I'm thinking about an individual and their whole life, you know, we're talking about things like lifestyle, health, career or business, personal growth, their interests, their relationships, whether they've got property, whatever it might be, it's success across all areas. I don't believe you have success in one area and then not success in other areas. So for me, I'm looking at that real balance picture and saying success is equal success across all areas that are important contextually. And that's the same, not just in life, but for business. And I see that the same for players as well and for coaches. So what are those key areas and what does success look like in each of those areas? So talk to people, teams and organizations around defining success. There's a wonderful psychometric assessment tool called the lifestyle's infantry, human synergistic lifestyle's infantry. And if you haven't come across that, if you're not familiar with that, really encourage you to have a look at that. That will give you some, some, I guess, perspectives on what are the elements if you like that are required to achieve success.

It's about constructive styles and that fundamentally there's four styles that are required to achieve success. It's about being achievement oriented, finding solutions to problems. The second one is about self actualizing. So being, you know, accepting where you're at at this point in time, wanting more, but accepting where you're at at this point in time and being okay with that. But looking for solutions to be better. It's about encouraging other people and helping people along the way. And it's also about being well networked and having good relationships and and always make that link back to success and the things that are required to achieve success. So I talk a little bit about that and that might be a useful resource to have a look at as well. So just a bit of context if you like to sort of set the scene around defining success and being very, very clear in terms of what we mean. So I'll now go into the document itself. And on the second page, you'll see that there's a graphic there which talks about my success map and I'll be looking down at this. So forgive me as I'm as I'm moving through it, but we talked a little bit about context, which is under step number one of that success map. There's really three steps to achieving success in my experience in working with people teams and organizations in the business and sporting space. And that fundamentally step number one, which we've kind of just talked about is having a very, very clear direction.

And within direction, I'm talking about things like a very clear vision, the word that I use on my map is intention, but I use those words interchangeably. But when we imagine what success looks like, what comes to mind? What do we see? What do we feel? What do we hear? It's all that sensory stuff that we talk about. But it's, again, starting with the end in mind and having a very, very clear picture of what success looks like. Often I'll talk with individuals and say, if you want to be healthy, if health is important to you, well, what does success look like? And people will say, well, I want to be fit. I want to be healthy. And so that's great. Fit is better than not fit. But what does fit look like? And then we'll talk about that a little bit more. And then we go down the rabbit hole a little bit further and say, well, I'm able to run distances and say, OK, well, what does that look like? And the further we define it, the closer we get to what that image really, really looks like. And you'll hear people say, well, I want to run 4Ks in 20 minutes. Some people say I want to run 4Ks in 30 minutes and 4Ks in 15 minutes and say, well, that's really great. We're getting some really, really good inputs there. But we need to be very, very clear on what we're talking about. Because if we say run 4Ks in 30 minutes, that's very different to run 4Ks in 15 minutes. At one level we're talking about close to the other level we're talking about casual running.

And so being very, very clear on what the vision is or alternatively intention, which is at step number four, is important at that direction step. And defining that as clearly as we can, having a real, real clear sense of it. And then the other element of that direction piece is mission or purpose. I use those words interchangeably as well to have a clear sense of what the purpose is along that journey. And so an example that I love to use here is if you think about, if you've got kids under five years of age or who have been at that age, or if you're wanting to, or you've been a kid anyway, so you'll understand that. It's got to feel like something that emotionally gets you up. It can't just be words on a page. And they're the critical things to get right at this first direction step. So as a coach, I'm looking at this going, right, what do I, what does that look like for me personally, for my player? What does that look like for them, for the team? If you've got physiotherapists or other team members around you, what does that look like? And really, really defining it in all the different buckets. So I just used an example of the vision for the kids. You know, we're talking about health relationships, career, they're the buckets for them. Then from your perspective as coach and then for the players and then for the team members, it's, you know, the buckets are going to be a little bit different or maybe those ones are included as well. But as I said, mission slash purpose, vision slash intention are really critical to get right. And you can see step number five in direction talks about, well, where are we at now? So we get that sense of where we're wanting to go. We also need to assess where we're at now. What does that gap look like? The next bit, which we'll talk about in just a moment, it's a strategy, but that direction says, step says, I've got a clear sense of where I'm going. I've got a clear sense of where I'm at and a clear sense of my purpose throughout that journey as well. And that's the critical bit. We get that right and clear at the starting point. The next bit becomes a lot easier.

So step number two then is all about strategy. And as you'll see from that graphic, there's really two parts of that strategy. Under step number eight, there's the task related elements. And under step number seven, there's the person related elements. And so what I'm saying there is that both are important. You can't just have the task related elements. I talk about that as things that we intellectualize and things that we need to more so manage. And I talk about the things on the person side as being the things that are more the emotional intelligence and the things that we have to lead. Both are required. You can have a great strategy, systems, processes, which I would put under task. But unless the individual is inspired to achieve it, unless they believe it and value it, then it's only going to be as good as the document that it's written on. So both are required. And interestingly, our brain is structured in that way. We've got the rational and the emotional. And so this sort of plays into that science a little bit as well. You see under the graphic as we go below step number eight, we're talking about tasks. It then breaks it up into those key things that I believe are important and from my experience are important. Defining the areas that we need to get results in. You can see there's an offshoot to the top right. There's some areas. So if we're looking at this at a life level, I've just suggested some buckets, some areas that are important at a life level.

We talked about those just a moment ago. But those areas might look very different on court or off court as a coach or as a player as a team. It might be about physical fitness, nutrition, psychology, technique, whatever it might be. So setting up those buckets very, very clearly as we start to then go down to look at the other elements that are under task. Because we start to talk about structures. So structures really talks about the people structure. So you've got your support team, then you can expand out that and talk about family structure, how that supports the player, the industry body, tennis Australia, how that supports the player. So we can start talking about what are those structures that link in and around the coach or the player and the team. And that's what we really mean by structures, having a real clear sense of what those are. Because out of that will come the relationship development stuff that we need to do and and stakeholder management and all those bits and pieces. There's systems as well. Those systems can be more macro. So we talk about systems over the course of the year or they can be more micro things like daily systems, rituals, things that we do when we get up out of bed and before we go to bed and all those bits and pieces. But on court, what are those systems that we use, performance review systems, whatever it might be. So we're really elaborating on those systems are critical and then we need to have integrity in those systems as well.

Again, this is just a mapping activity to begin with and then we can flesh that out to design strategy but also use it as an assessment tool to say, well, how are we performing in some of these things as well. And also getting alignment, making sure that we're all seeing the bits that are involved in strategy. We're aligned on that. There's resources, of course, by that we mean financial people information resources or what are the resources that we need within the strategy people resources. I think that's obvious in terms of the people that are important to achieve success, and then tools, leadership tools models, whatever it might be any, any, those conceptual tools or physical tools are required so literally equipment shoes, blankets, all that stuff, and then non physical stuff, the more the psychology tools about mindset and psychology. So what we have under step eight then is all the tasks related elements and from that we would, you know, to the extent that you want to document that and put that down on paper, you can, but at least it gives you a framework to start thinking about the things that you need to put in place design, implement, review and assess how you're performing against that so becomes a really good map to do all of those things and get on the same page. As I said earlier, it's not just the, it's not the only bit because there's the left hand side or step number seven which is person.

Let me share an example here. And that is to the little comic strip Hagar the horrible. And it's a, it's a classic. It's got Hagar in a boat with all of his soldiers, and they're at the shore.
